# 5.2: Pickup and Delivery Routing

ISE 754: Logistics Engineering, Fall 2026

Consolidation is easy when shipments share an origin or destination; it is much harder when each has its own.

No new Julia packages used.

New Logjam functions used

- isorigin: Determine which positions in a route are origins (first occurrence).
- mincostinsert: Insert a shipment into a route at the minimum cost position.
- pairwisesavings: Calculate savings from combining pairs of single-shipment routes.
- rte2loc: Convert a route to a location sequence.
- rteTC: Calculate the total cost of a route.
- savings: Construct routes for a Pickup and Delivery Problem (PDP) using a savings-ordered insertion heuristic.

Companion script

5-rte-2.jl (shmtNC30-xy.csv), runnable Julia extracted from the lecture’s code blocks.

## 1. Route sequencing

Two simple construction procedures, mincostinsert and savings, along with the twoopt improvement of Lecture 5.1, can be used for most routing applications, including pickup and delivery routing, where each shipment has its own origin and destination. Pickup and delivery routing covers alternatives (d) and (e) of Fig. 1 in Lecture 5.1, in which each shipment is picked up at its own origin and delivered to its own destination, and the truck need not return to where it started.

Half a dozen other construction procedures for the TSP could easily be added, though there are few improvement procedures beyond 2-opt; the savings procedure works as well or better in most cases. It is also much more robust, since it makes no assumptions: many of the others work only for metric distances, or only under certain constraints on the TSP, and the savings procedure has none of those limitations. Like the older methods of routing, it works in all cases, where the more specialized procedures, though more efficient in particular cases, are in general not as robust. And it can handle the more general case of pickup and delivery routing. The classic TSP is peddling or collecting, two of the routing alternatives of Lecture 5.1, where a route is just the sequence of its stops, essentially a permutation. That representation does not carry over to interleaved routes, whose shipments have different origins and different destinations, though the savings procedure can fairly easily be adapted to them. What else is needed to handle that more complicated case is the subject of the sections that follow.

When each shipment can have its own origin and destination, a location sequence is no longer adequate to represent a route, as it was for a tour in Lecture 5.1, whose permutation $\pi$ sufficed because every stop was a delivery from, or a pickup for, the depot. Fig. 1 illustrates three such shipments. Shipped independently, shipment 1 travels 300 miles from its origin at location 1 to its destination at location 2, shipment 2 travels 250 miles from location 3 to 4, and shipment 3 travels 275 miles from location 5 to 6.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 1: three shipments and the roads between their locations
P = [0.0 0.0; 4.0 0.0; 0.35 0.75; 3.65 0.75;  # locations 1 to 6
     0.35 -1.1; 3.65 -1.1]
rn = 0.17  # location radius, data units
links = [(1, 2, 300), (3, 4, 250), (5, 6, 275), (1, 3, 30), (4, 2, 30),
         (1, 5, 60), (6, 2, 60)]  # road links, with their miles
# points along a curve from p to q, bowed toward c
curvepts(p, c, q; n = 60) = [(1 - s)^2 .* p .+ 2(1 - s) * s .* c .+
                             s^2 .* q for s in range(0, 1, length = n)]
# the part of a curve outside the circles around a and b, cut on each
# outline
function clipnodes(pts, a, b; r = rn)
    ins(x, o) = hypot((x .- o)...) < r
    function cross(u, v, o)  # where u to v crosses the outline around o
        lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
        for _ in 1:40
            mid = (lo + hi) / 2
            ins(u .+ mid .* (v .- u), o) ? (lo = mid) : (hi = mid)
        end
        return u .+ hi .* (v .- u)
    end
    i = findfirst(x -> !ins(x, a), pts)
    j = findlast(x -> !ins(x, b), pts)
    return vcat([cross(pts[i-1], pts[i], a)], pts[i:j],
                [cross(pts[j+1], pts[j], b)])
end
function arrowline!(ax, pts, col; lw = 2.5)  # its tip on the last point
    lines!(ax, first.(pts), last.(pts); color = col, linewidth = lw)
    j = findlast(x -> hypot((pts[end] .- x)...) > 0.25, pts)
    u, v = pts[j], pts[end]
    arrows2d!(ax, [u[1]], [u[2]], [v[1] - u[1]], [v[2] - u[2]];
              color = col, shaftwidth = lw,
              tipwidth = 11, tiplength = 11)
end
function drawlink!(ax, i, j, d)  # a road, dotted, with its miles
    p, q = P[i, :], P[j, :]
    seg = clipnodes(curvepts(p, (p .+ q) ./ 2, q), p, q)
    lines!(ax, first.(seg), last.(seg); color = redc, linestyle = :dot,
           linewidth = 1.5)
    m, long = (p .+ q) ./ 2, abs(q[1] - p[1]) > 1
    side = m[1] < 2 ? -1 : 1  # a short link's miles beside it
    text!(ax, m[1], m[2]; text = string(d), color = redc, fontsize = 13,
          align = long ? (:center, :top) :
                  (side < 0 ? :right : :left, :center),
          offset = long ? (0, -4) : (6side, 0))
end
function drawshipment!(ax, b, e, label)  # bowed above its road
    p, q = P[b, :], P[e, :]
    c = [(p[1] + q[1]) / 2, p[2] + 0.38]
    arrowline!(ax, clipnodes(curvepts(p, c, q), p, q), bluec)
    top = (p .+ q) ./ 4 .+ c ./ 2  # the curve's highest point
    text!(ax, top[1], top[2]; text = label, color = bluec,
          fontsize = 13, align = (:center, :bottom), offset = (0, 3))
end
function drawnodes!(ax, idx)  # locations, over everything
    for i in idx
        poly!(ax, Circle(Point2f(P[i, 1], P[i, 2]), rn); color = :white,
              strokecolor = ink, strokewidth = 1.5)
        text!(ax, P[i, 1], P[i, 2]; text = string(i), color = ink,
              fontsize = 13, align = (:center, :center))
    end
end
# an arrowhead partway along each leg of a route through x, y, so its
# direction shows; on a map, x and y are longitude and latitude, and
# each leg is taken as the map's Mercator projection draws it
merc(φ) = log(tand(45 + φ / 2))
function legarrows!(ax, x, y; color, onmap = false, at = 0.55,
                    size = 12, every = 1)
    Y = onmap ? merc.(y) : y
    for i in 1:every:length(x)-1
        dx, dy = x[i+1] - x[i], Y[i+1] - Y[i]
        dx == dy == 0 && continue          # a location visited twice
        xm, ym = x[i] + at * dx, Y[i] + at * dy
        scatter!(ax, [xm], [onmap ? 2atand(exp(ym)) - 90 : ym];
                 marker = :rtriangle, markersize = size,
                 rotation = atan(dy, onmap ? deg2rad(dx) : dx),
                 color = color isa AbstractVector ? color[i] : color)
    end
end
# the shipments loaded (L) and unloaded (U) at location i: (L1,2:U3)
function ldlabel(i, sh)
    L, U = findall(==(i), sh.b), findall(==(i), sh.e)
    parts = [isempty(L) ? "" : "L" * join(L, ","),
             isempty(U) ? "" : "U" * join(U, ",")]
    s = join(filter(!isempty, parts), ":")
    return isempty(s) ? "" : "($s)"
end
let fig = Figure(size = (560, 330))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; aspect = DataAspect())
    hidedecorations!(ax); hidespines!(ax)
    foreach(l -> drawlink!(ax, l...), links)
    for (k, (b, e)) in enumerate([(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)])
        drawshipment!(ax, b, e, "Shipment $k")
    end
    drawnodes!(ax, 1:6)
    xlims!(ax, -0.5, 4.5); ylims!(ax, -1.5, 1.25)
    fig
end
```

Figure 1: Three-shipment example. Each shipment (blue) travels from its origin to its destination; the dotted links (red) are the roads between the locations, with their miles.

One route that carries all three shipments on one truck is described by its shipment, route and location sequences:

$$
\begin{array}{rclcl} L &=& ( y_{1} , \ldots , y_{n} ) &=& ( 1 , 2 , 3 ) \\ R &=& ( z_{1} , \ldots , z_{2 n} ) &=& ( 3 , 1 , 2 , 2 , 1 , 3 ) \\ X &=& ( x_{1} , \ldots , x_{2 n} ) &=& ( 5 , 1 , 3 , 4 , 2 , 6 )\end{array}
\tag{1}
$$

where

- $L$ = $n$-element shipment sequence
- $R$ = $2n$-element route sequence
- $X$ = $2n$-element location (node) sequence
- $n$ = number of shipments in the load.

The TSP and the classic vehicle routing problem have a single origin and destination, the depot: all of the routes start at one point and end at one point. In practice many routing problems have no depot. A national trucking company, for example, might carry blood plasma that has passed its expiration date for transfusion from the clinics where it was donated to the medical facilities that use it as a raw material for drug products; its trucks start and stop all over the country, and routing code written for a depot does not work when each shipment has its own origin and destination. In Fig. 1, the three shipments all go in the same general direction. Done point to point, their cost is just the sum of their individual costs, whether distance or cost; but there are obvious savings if one truck could pick up all three shipments and drop each one off at its destination. The way a route was represented for the TSP does not map over. There a route was the sequence of customers starting at the depot, a permutation of their indices, and any permutation was a valid route, because everything delivered came from one location or, in collecting, everything picked up ended at one final destination. When the shipments have different origins and destinations, the representation has to change. Instead of a permutation, a route is a vector in which each shipment is indicated by its number, which appears twice: the first time it is picked up, and the second time it is dropped off at its destination. The route (3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3) picks up shipment 3 first, then shipment 1, then shipment 2, and then drops off shipments 2, 1 and 3. A minus sign on each drop-off is unnecessary, since the order from left to right tells which occurrence is the pickup and which the drop-off; and with a sign, moving the numbers around, as 2-opt improvement does, could put a drop-off before its pickup, which an unsigned route cannot. So there are three sequences. The shipment sequence lists the shipments being considered, here 1, 2 and 3, without saying in what order they are picked up and delivered; the route gives the actual sequence of pickups and deliveries; and the location sequence gives, for every element of the route, the location at which that pickup or delivery occurs. Here every pickup and delivery is at a distinct location, but the same location could be the pickup or the delivery of different shipments, and the representation handles that easily. Many of the construction and improvement procedures map over to it, changed a little but with the same basic logic. The route above costs 60 + 30 + 250 + 30 + 60 = 430, against 825 for the three shipments done independently point to point, a saving of almost 50%.

The procedure to determine the minimum cost route sequence takes the sequence $L = \left(y_1,\ldots,y_n\right)$ of $n$ shipments in a load as input and outputs a $2n$-element route sequence $R = \left(z_1,\ldots,z_{2n}\right)$, representing the sequence in which the loading and unloading of each shipment occurs, so as to minimize the total cost to travel from the loading of the first shipment to the unloading of the last shipment in the route. The first occurrence of $z_j = y_i$ in $R$ indicates the loading of shipment $y_i$, and the second occurrence of $z_k = y_i$ indicates its unloading, where $j < k$. Each element $z_i$ of route sequence $R$ has a corresponding location $x_i$, $X = \left(x_1,\ldots,x_{2n}\right)$, representing either the origin or destination location of the shipment. A $2n$-element route $R$ has $2n-1$ segments, where each segment consists of a consecutive pair of elements in $R$, $\left(z_i, z_{i+1}\right)$. The total cost of $R$ is the sum of the cost of each of its segments. Given the costs $c_{ij}$ between all pairs of locations $i$ and $j$,

$$
c(R)=\sum_{i=1}^{2n-1} c_{x_i,\,x_{i+1}}
\tag{2}
$$

where

- $c(R)$ = total cost of route $R$
- $x_i$ = location at which element $z_i$ of $R$ is loaded or unloaded
- $c_{ij}$ = cost between locations $i$ and $j$.

Eq. 2 represents the cost of route $R$. For example, referring to Fig. 1, the route sequence $\left(3,1,2,2,1,3\right)$ would correspond to travel from location 5 after loading shipment 3 to location 1 to load shipment 1, to location 3 to load 2, to 4 to unload 2, to 2 to unload 1, and to 6 to unload 3. The total cost of the route is 430, where $c_{5,1} =$ 60, etc.

In Fig. 1 the cost of each shipment can be taken as its distance, at \$1 per mile, so shipment 1 costs 300 as an independent shipment, shipment 2 costs 250 and shipment 3 costs 275. Since the shipments do not all start from the same depot, each could always hire a carrier to pick it up and deliver it, and that is always an alternative. If the shipments are small enough to fit easily onto one truck, putting all of them on one truck makes sense if it saves total distance traveled, and the question is then which origin to start from, which shipment to load first, second and third, and how to deliver them. With $n$ shipments the route sequence is twice as long, $2n$, where a TSP of $n$ stops had a sequence of $n$, or $n + 1$ with the depot, so the effort is essentially doubled. Each route is not entered by hand: a construction procedure creates it, since with shipments all over the place there are many alternatives, and the computer does the hard work of finding the best. As a freebie, the 2-opt procedure of Lecture 5.1, designed for a permutation, works just as well on a route, because each number appears twice and carries no sign: flipping the middle portion of a route still leaves each shipment loaded before it is unloaded, though Sec. 2 shows that it can leave the truck empty. The location sequence is like the tour of the TSP, the actual locations visited; but where a TSP has one depot and every other location a drop-off or a pickup, here shipment 2, for example, starts at location 3, its own warehouse, and is shipped to a customer at location 4. Procedures for routing have to deal with both sequences, where the TSP had only one, and that restriction is why the TSP handles only peddling or collecting, not mixtures of pickups and deliveries at different places, as most routing problems other than the classic TSP have, such as those of a trucking company with customers all over the place. What follows covers only the mechanics of constructing such routes, leaving the capacity of trucks and the other constraints, such as time windows, to the vehicle routing problem of Lecture 5.3. Constraints only reduce what is possible, so this is the best case, the unconstrained vehicle routing problem. Nor is it obvious that all three shipments always belong on one route: if shipment 3 were far away, it would probably be better off on its own truck, with the other two combined. Shipments clustered geographically are the ones worth combining, and the representation handles the cases where combining does not make sense. That is why the term independent shipment is used: a shipment is independent of a consolidated route, and it is shipped TL or LTL, whichever is cheaper, the choice of Lecture 3.2.

The route sequencing problem is a generalization of the traveling salesman problem and simple heuristics can be used to provide reasonably good solutions. In order to make the route sequencing procedure especially simple and fast, an online procedure is used that takes as input only the current route sequence and the shipment to be added to the sequence. This is opposed to a more time-consuming offline procedure that would use all of the shipments to construct the route sequence. While an offline procedure can sometimes produce better results and would make the resulting route independent of the order in which shipments are added to the route, it requires extra time.

Route sequencing is stated as a model in Model 1. It generalizes the TSP of Model 1 in Lecture 5.1, which is the case in which every shipment is loaded at one location, peddling, or unloaded at one, collecting, and a truck begins and ends its route there, as in Ex. 6(d), so that the route reduces to a permutation. It keeps the TSP’s leave and enter constraints, those of the linear assignment problem of Model 1 in Lecture 4.2, on the route’s stops, opens its single tour into a single route that need not return to its start, and adds precedence; Secs. 2 and 3 formulate its two construction procedures.

minimize: total cost of ~~a tour through every node~~ one route that loads and unloads every shipment of a load

solve for:
(a) ~~tour~~ route, a sequence ~~that visits each node exactly once and returns to its starting node~~ of stops, the loading and the unloading of each shipment.

subject to:
(a) Leave: each ~~node~~ stop is left exactly once, except the last;
(b) Enter: each ~~node~~ stop is entered exactly once, except the first;
(c) Single ~~tour~~ route: the arcs used form one connected ~~cycle~~ path through all the ~~nodes~~ stops, not several, the truck carrying at least one shipment along each;
(d) Precedence: each shipment is loaded before it is unloaded.

assumptions:
(a) each shipment has its own origin and destination;
(b) ~~arc costs~~ costs between locations are given and need not be symmetric;
(c) cost of a ~~tour~~ route is the sum of the costs of its ~~arcs, including the return to the start~~ segments, from the loading of the first shipment to the unloading of the last.

Model 1: Route sequencing

Generalization of Model 1: Traveling salesman problem in Lecture 5.1

Constraint (c) is what defines a route: no segment of it has the truck empty. A segment on which the truck is empty divides it into two routes; otherwise a truck traveling for months on the road, with long gaps of empty travel between its shipments, would all be one route. The point of view is also typically the shipper’s, not the carrier’s: only the carrier is concerned with minimizing deadhead, the empty travel between routes, and what happens between routes is a problem for the carrier, outside the focus of this course.

Example 1: Three shipments on one route

Determine the cost of the route $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$ for the three shipments of Fig. 1, by hand and in Julia, how it compares with shipping them as independent shipments, and the least costly of every route.

Example 1(a): By hand

Determine the route’s cost from its location sequence in Eq. 1 and the costs of Fig. 1.

With the location sequence $X$ of Eq. 1, its cost by Eq. 2 is:

$$
c ( R ) = \sum_{i = 1}^{2 n - 1} c_{x_{i} , x_{i + 1}} = 60 + 30 + 250 + 30 + 60 = 430
\tag{3}
$$

The five segments of Eq. 3 add up to the route’s cost, and when Ex. 1(b) computes the same 430 in code, an independent route agrees with the hand sum, a Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2. Their total is also bounded on both sides, a Bounds check: the route carries shipment 1 from location 1 to location 2, so it cannot cost less than that shipment’s own 300, and it is worth having only if it costs less than the $300 + 250 + 275 = 825$ of the three shipments done independently.

The route $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$ visits locations $(5, 1, 3, 4, 2, 6)$ and costs 430, against 825 for the three independent shipments.

Example 1(b): In Julia

Determine the same location sequence and cost with Logjam’s isorigin, rte2loc and rteTC, from the costs $D$ between the six locations.

The costs between the locations are the shortest distances on the links of Fig. 1:

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 300 & 30 & 280 & 60 & 335 \\
300 & 0 & 280 & 30 & 335 & 60 \\
30 & 280 & 0 & 250 & 90 & 340 \\
280 & 30 & 250 & 0 & 340 & 90 \\
60 & 335 & 90 & 340 & 0 & 275 \\
335 & 60 & 340 & 90 & 275 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\tag{4}
$$

where

- $D$ = costs between the locations, its row $i$ and column $j$ the cost $c_{ij}$ from location $i$ to location $j$.

Code block 2 computes $D$ of Eq. 4 as Lecture 4.1 computes the distances between cities on a road network: the seven roads of Fig. 1, each two-way, form a network of the six locations, and Dijkstra’s procedure, run from each location, gives its shortest distance to every other. It then enters the shipments, each a row with its origin b and destination e, as Logjam’s routing functions read them:

```julia
# Code block 2: the costs between the six locations, and the shipments
using Graphs, SimpleWeightedGraphs
i = [1, 3, 5, 1, 4, 1, 6]              # one end of each road
j = [2, 4, 6, 3, 2, 5, 2]              # its other end
w = [300, 250, 275, 30, 30, 60, 60]    # its miles
g = SimpleWeightedGraph(i, j, w)       # a network of two-way roads
D, _ = shortestpaths(g, weights(g), nv(g))  # from every location
D = Int.(D)                            # whole miles
sh = DataFrame(b = [1, 3, 5], e = [2, 4, 6])  # origin, destination
D

```

- 1 shortestpaths(g, weights(g), n) runs Dijkstra’s procedure from each of the first n nodes, here all six, and returns the shortest distances between them and the predecessors, of which only the distances are kept, as in Lecture 4.1; Int.(D) then gives the distances as the whole miles they are.

```text
6×6 Matrix{Int64}:
   0  300   30  280   60  335
 300    0  280   30  335   60
  30  280    0  250   90  340
 280   30  250    0  340   90
  60  335   90  340    0  275
 335   60  340   90  275    0
```

Code block 3 marks which elements of the route are loadings, the first occurrence of each shipment, translates the route into its location sequence, and costs each segment and the whole route:

```julia
# Code block 3: the route's loadings, location sequence and cost
R = [3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3]
@show isorigin(R)  # true where a shipment is loaded
@show X = rte2loc(R, sh)  # the location of each element
@show segcost(X, D)                           # the cost of each segment
@show rteTC(R, sh, D)                         # the route's cost
@show sum(D[sh.b[k], sh.e[k]] for k in 1:3);  # three independent
```

```text
isorigin(R) = Bool[1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]
X = rte2loc(R, sh) = Any[5, 1, 3, 4, 2, 6]
segcost(X, D) = [60, 30, 250, 30, 60]
rteTC(R, sh, D) = 430
sum((D[sh.b[k], sh.e[k]] for k = 1:3)) = 825
```

rteTC is the sum of segcost over the location sequence rte2loc gives, which is Eq. 2.

Logjam’s rteTC gives the same 430, and the three independent shipments cost 825.

Example 1(c): Every route

Determine the least costly of every route of the three shipments, by brute force.

With only three shipments, the cost of every route can be computed, and the least costly of them is the optimum that the construction procedures of Secs. 2 and 3 are compared with. Each of the three shipments appears twice in a route, so there are $6!/(2!\,2!\,2!) = 90$ distinct orderings of $(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)$, and with $n$ shipments there are $(2n)!/2^n$; in each, the first appearance of a shipment is its loading. Not every ordering is a route, though: in 30 of the 90, such as $(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)$, the truck is empty on a segment, having unloaded every shipment it loaded before it loads the next, which by constraint (c) of Model 1 makes two or three routes, so 60 of the orderings are routes. Lecture 5.1 closed by expecting interleaved pickups and deliveries to need hard construction; written as this unsigned route vector, with no constraints, a route is still easy to construct, since loading every shipment before unloading any always gives one, so pickup and delivery is again a case of easy construction, and hard construction returns with the constraints of Lecture 5.3. The multiset_permutations function of the Combinatorics package lists exactly those orderings: given a collection in which elements repeat, here each shipment twice, it gives each distinct ordering of it once, where permutations would list all $6! = 720$ orderings of the six elements, the same ordering eight times over. Code block 4 keeps the orderings that are routes, those on which the truck always carries a shipment, and finds the cost of each, one at a time, as Code block 19 of Lecture 5.1 does for every tour:

```julia
# Code block 4: all 60 routes by brute force
using Combinatorics
rtesegsum(r, x) =
    cumsum(x[r] .* ifelse.(isorigin(r), 1, -1))[1:end-1]
v = [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]
rtes = (r for r ∈ multiset_permutations(v, 6)
        if all(>(0), rtesegsum(r, ones(3))))
TCᵒ, rᵒ = minimum((rteTC(r, sh, D), r) for r ∈ rtes)

@show length(multiset_permutations(v, 6))   # the orderings
@show length(collect(rtes))                 # the routes
@show TCᵒ                                   # the cheapest of them
@show count(rteTC(r, sh, D) == TCᵒ for r ∈ rtes)  # how many that cheap
rᵒ                                          # the cheapest route

```

- 1 rtesegsum gives the cumulative sum of a value of each shipment over each segment of a route: isorigin is true for each element that is a loading, the first appearance of its shipment, as Code block 10 shows, so the value is added at the shipment’s loading and subtracted at its unloading. With a 1 for each shipment it gives the number of shipments on the truck over each segment, and with each shipment’s weight it would give the weight on board.
- 2 multiset_permutations(v, 6) gives the distinct orderings of all 6 elements of v, each once, though shipments 1, 2 and 3 each appear twice in it: 90 of them, against the 720 of permutations(v). The parentheses make rtes a generator, which produces the routes one at a time as the next line finds their costs, rather than storing all 60 first.
- 3 The if keeps the 60 orderings on which the truck carries at least one shipment over every segment, the routes.
- 4 Each route is paired with its cost, and minimum compares the pairs by cost first, so it returns the cheapest cost together with its route, as Code block 5 of Lecture 5.1 does for tours.

```text
length(multiset_permutations(v, 6)) = 90
length(collect(rtes)) = 60
TCᵒ = 430
count((rteTC(r, sh, D) == TCᵒ for r = rtes)) = 1
```

```text
6-element Vector{Int64}:
 3
 1
 2
 2
 1
 3
```

The least costly of all 60 routes is the route of Ex. 1(a), $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$, at 430, and no other route costs as little.

The optimum of the 60 routes is $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$, at 430.

Location indices in a location vector should range from 1 to the number of unique locations. This allows correct indexing into a distance matrix. Code block 5, for example, shows how to convert shipment origin and destination zip codes into a location vector.

In many problems, the information about where the origins and destinations are has to be translated into location vectors, that is, into indices that range from 1 to the number of unique locations. The reason is that the routing procedures, trying all the different possible beginning and end points for a route, look up each segment in a matrix of distances or travel times, which needs an index for each location. The four shipments of Code block 5 have four origin and four destination zip codes, but because of duplication there are only four unique ones, so each zip code is mapped to its unique location. The origin and destination zip codes are put in one list, the unique zip codes in it are found, without the duplicates, and the location indices run from 1 to the number of unique zip codes; each shipment’s beginning point b and endpoint e is then the index of its zip code among them. The first shipment, for example, begins at location 2, zip code 27606, the second of the unique zip codes, and ends at location 4. This is almost the plumbing of routing, one of the low-level things, but there is no obvious way of doing it, and the code is worth keeping as an example. A function could hide it all on the assumption that the locations are always zip codes, but seeing it done this way makes it easier to adapt to other ways of representing points: if the origins and destinations were given by longitude and latitude to three digits of accuracy, say, two of them within some threshold distance of each other could be taken as the same location before the indices are assigned. From the routing procedure’s point of view, what matters is that with the beginning and end points as indices 1 through 4, a procedure trying different ways of inserting shipments into routes can look up the corresponding distance or travel time in the matrix.

As an example, four shipments are known only by the zip codes of their origins and destinations, as a shipper’s records might give them: from Raleigh, North Carolina (27606) to Detroit (48234), from Gainesville, Florida (32606) to Cary, North Carolina (27518), from Detroit to Gainesville, and from Gainesville to Detroit. Code block 5 puts the origin and destination zip codes of the four shipments in one list, keeps each zip code once, sorted, and gives each shipment’s origin and destination as its index b and e among them; the zip codes’ centroids then give the distance matrix the indices look into:

```julia
# Code block 5: zip codes to locations, and the distances between them
shz = DataFrame(orig = [27606, 32606, 48234, 32606],
                dest = [48234, 27518, 32606, 48234])
zips = sort(unique([shz.orig; shz.dest]))  # each zip code once
loc = 1:length(zips)                       # the location indices
shz.b = indexin(shz.orig, zips)            # each origin's location
shz.e = indexin(shz.dest, zips)            # each destination's
z = uszcta5()
XY = Matrix(z[indexin(zips, z.ZCTA5), [:LON, :LAT]])
Dz = dists(XY, XY, :mi) * 1.2              # road miles, circuity 1.2
@show DataFrame(loc = loc, zip = zips)
@show shz
round.(Dz, digits = 2)
```

A comparison of the same kind, three shipments first considered as three independent shipments and then combined on one route that uses the same truck, is the analysis a carrier or trucking company would make: it has three different shipments, for which it would at least initially task three different trucks, and it would also consider what happens if one truck carries several of the shipments at the same time.

The route of Code block 10 is not meant to be optimal; it is just a route to work with, and any route will do: a random route is essentially two random permutations mixed together, as the random tours of Lecture 5.1 were one. The first of the functions identifies which elements of a route are origins and which are destinations, since each shipment’s number appears twice: it gives the Boolean value true for the elements that are pickups, and its negation is then true for the deliveries. It uses Julia’s set data structure to keep track of which shipments have been seen: a shipment not yet seen is a pickup and is added to the set, and one already seen is a delivery. The next function does a lot of the work of the procedures: given a route, it translates it into its location sequence, using one of Julia’s most useful features, an ifelse that can be broadcast, so that for a pickup it takes the shipment’s beginning field b and otherwise its ending field e. This is critical, because whenever there is a route, its location sequence can immediately be found, and the location sequence is what is then used to look up the cost of each segment of the route. That is what the segment cost function does, the same segcost that Lecture 5.1 used for a tour, here given the location sequence: it picks out the element of the cost matrix for each segment of the route. Added up, they give 916.86, an improvement over the 1,006.18 of the three independent shipments, even though the route is not necessarily optimal.

The five segment costs of Code block 12 are numbers picked from the matrix: the first segment, from location 1 to location 3, is 264, the entry in row 1 and column 3. The matrix here is the distance matrix D, but in general it can be a cost, which is why the functions call it C, and it is given the distance matrix because here distance and cost are the same. Most realistically the cost of a routing problem is the travel time, written T; it is rarely dollars, because the same trucks are used and their cost per mile is about the same, so that distance is a good substitute, but time is usually what constrains a route: hours-of-service rules, for example, allow a truck driver no more than 11 hours of driving, and a route may also have a maximum distance. So generically the term is cost, but it is usually a time or a distance, not dollars. Route total cost, rteTC, puts route-to-location and segment cost together: from the route, the shipments and the cost matrix it finds the location sequence, costs its segments and sums them, 916.86 for this route. It is the main worker bee. Every constraint is put into the route total cost, so the 2-opt, savings and minimum cost insertion procedures need no change when constraints are added. Here it is unconstrained and only adds up the segments; but with a limit of, say, 1,000 miles on a route, it could return a cost of infinity for a route that exceeds the limit, and in the savings procedure, which looks only at positive savings, an infinite cost of consolidating gives a savings of minus infinity. It is the same idea as the infinite cost that the maximin location of Lecture 2.2, Sec. 4, gives a point outside the region it must stay in, used in a routing context, and none of the routing code has to change. To use it, Code block 14 defines a one-line function rTDh of the route alone, since the distance matrix and the shipments do not change; it locks in their current values, and the h, for handle, marks it as a one-line function that does a calculation. The single-shipment route of shipment 1, $(1, 1)$, a pickup in Raleigh and a delivery in Athens, is a valid route whose cost is just the distance from location 1 to location 2 in the matrix, with nothing recalculated.

```julia
# Code block 14: the costs of some single- and multi-shipment routes
rTDh(rte) = rteTC(rte, sh, D)
@show rTDh([1, 1])
@show rTDh([1, 1]) + rTDh([2, 2]) + rTDh([3, 3])
@show rTDh([1, 2, 2, 1]) + rTDh([3, 3])
@show rTDh([1, 2, 1, 2]) + rTDh([3, 3])
@show rTDh([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3])
@show rTDh([1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2])
```

A route that interleaves the first two shipments, $(1, 2, 1, 2)$, with shipment 3 on a single-shipment route beats shipping all three independently, and the route $(1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2)$ of Code block 10, which carries all three, is the cheapest of those tried. Which route is cheapest of all is what the construction procedures of Secs. 2 and 3 determine.

Shipped independently, the three shipments travel 1,006.18 mi; of the routes tried, $(1, 2, 1, 3, 3, 2)$ is the shortest, at 916.86 mi.

## 2. Minimum cost insertion

There are two types of routing procedure, depending on the application. Most of the time these problems are thought of in an offline mode: all of the candidate shipments are available at one time, and from that group the best thing to do can be determined. But sometimes shipments come in with no advance knowledge of what will be available: the truck starts operating with one shipment, and while it is on the road a second shipment asks to be picked up, and before what to do with that one is determined a third arrives. The truck might be going off in a direction that, in retrospect, with all of the information available at the beginning, would have been done in a different order at less cost or less distance. Without that information, the procedure is an online procedure.

Online procedure: a procedure that adds a shipment to an existing route as it becomes available. Its example is Insert and Improve, which, for each shipment, inserts it where it has the least increase in cost for the route and then improves the route (mincostinsert → twoopt).

Offline procedure: a procedure that considers all shipments to determine the order in which each is added to the route. Its example is Savings and Improve, which, using all shipments, determines the insert ordering based on “savings,” and then improves the final route (savings → twoopt).

Minimum cost insertion is not only the online procedure: savings, the offline one, uses it to merge two routes, inserting each shipment of one into the other (Sec. 3), so it is needed even when every shipment is known at once.

Of the two techniques used here, the savings procedure works only offline, with all of the data available, since it is a way of selecting which shipments are the best ones to start a route with, as Sec. 3 shows. Minimum cost insertion works every time a new shipment is given for whatever the existing route is: it finds the best place in that route to add the one shipment, giving another route with the new shipment in it, and when another shipment comes minutes later it can be added the same way. It is like a greedy procedure, as in Lecture 4.1, always taking the next optimal step, so the route it finishes with is probably not as good as that of an offline procedure that has all of the data. These are two areas of application, and neither is better than the other.

Fig. 3 shows the procedure’s two steps, inserting a second shipment into a route and then a third:

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 15: the positions minimum cost insertion tries
let  # set in the lecture math's serif, as is the route (1, 2, 2, 1)
    fig = Figure(size = (470, 542), figure_padding = 4,
                 fonts = (; regular = Makie.MathTeXEngine.texfont()))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; aspect = DataAspect())
    hidedecorations!(ax); hidespines!(ax)
    w, dy = 0.78, 0.62  # a column's width, a row's height
    X(c) = c * w
    # position (i, j) loads the shipment in gap i, unloads it in gap j;
    # each gap has two columns, and the route's stops are at 3, 6, ...
    function slots(i, j)
        sx(g, s) = 3(g - 1) + s
        return i == j ? (sx(i, 1), sx(i, 2)) : (sx(i, 2), sx(j, 1))
    end
    # a table's rules, its column rules, and its subcaption below
    function frame!(y0, yb, xr, cap; ncol = 0.0)
        for yy in (y0 + 0.5dy, y0 - 0.5dy, yb)
            lines!(ax, [X(-1.25), xr], [yy, yy]; color = ink,
                   linewidth = 1)
        end
        lines!(ax, [X(-0.2), X(-0.2)], [y0 + 0.5dy, yb]; color = ink,
               linewidth = 1)
        ncol > 0 && lines!(ax, [ncol, ncol], [y0 + 0.5dy, yb];
                           color = ink, linewidth = 1)
        text!(ax, (X(-1.25) + xr) / 2, yb - 0.12; text = cap,
              fontsize = 15, color = ink, align = (:center, :top))
    end
    # bad: the rows that are not routes, a red × in place of their cost
    function postable!(route, k, pos, y0, best, bad, cap)
        m = length(route)
        stops = X.(3 .* (1:m))
        ncol = X(3m + 2.6)                 # the rule before the costs
        xr = ncol + 1.25
        text!(ax, stops, fill(y0, m); text = string.(route),
              fontsize = 16, color = ink, align = (:center, :center))
        for (r, (i, j)) in enumerate(pos)  # one row per position
            y = y0 - r * dy
            r == best && poly!(ax, Rect(X(-1.25), y - dy / 2,
                                        xr - X(-1.25), dy);
                               color = (bluec, 0.14))  # the least
            text!(ax, X(-0.7), y; text = string(r), fontsize = 16,
                  color = ink, align = (:center, :center))
            scatter!(ax, stops, fill(y, m); color = ink, markersize = 6)
            text!(ax, X.(collect(slots(i, j))), [y, y];
                  text = fill("$k", 2), fontsize = 16, color = ink,
                  align = (:center, :center))
            r in bad ?
                text!(ax, ncol + 0.15, y; text = "×", fontsize = 20,
                      color = redc, align = (:left, :center)) :
                text!(ax, ncol + 0.15, y; text = L"c_{%$r}",
                      fontsize = 17, color = r == best ? bluec : ink,
                      align = (:left, :center))
            r == best && scatter!(ax, [ncol + 0.95], [y];
                                  marker = :star5, markersize = 15,
                                  color = bluec)
        end
        yb = y0 - (length(pos) + 0.5) * dy
        frame!(y0, yb, xr, cap; ncol)
        return yb
    end
    # rows 1 and 6 of (a), the end and the front, leave the truck empty
    pos2 = [(3, 3), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 3), (1, 2), (1, 1)]
    yb = postable!([1, 1], 2, pos2, 0.0, 3, [1, 6],
                   "(a) Shipment 2 inserted into the route (1, 1)")
    pos3 = [(i, j) for i in 1:5 for j in i:5 if (i, j) != (1, 1)]
    push!(pos3, (1, 1))                    # the front last, as in (a)
    yb3 = postable!([1, 2, 2, 1], 3, pos3, yb - 1.25, 4, [14, 15],
                    "(b) Shipment 3 inserted into the route " *
                    "(1, 2, 2, 1)")
    xr = X(3 * 4 + 2.6) + 1.25             # the right edge of (b)
    xlims!(ax, -1.4w, xr + 0.1); ylims!(ax, yb3 - 0.7, 0.5)
    fig
end
```

Figure 3: Minimum cost insertion, a • marking a stop of the route and a red × a position that is not a route, since the truck is empty between the shipments: (a) shipment 2 inserted into the route $(1, 1)$ at each of the six positions of its loading and unloading, four of them routes, at costs $c_2$ to $c_5$; (b) if $c_3$ is the least (blue, starred), shipment 3 inserted into the route $(1, 2, 2, 1)$ at each of its 15 positions, 13 of them routes. If $c_4$ is then the least (starred), the route found is $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$.

Minimum cost insertion is in some sense like 2-opt, but it works on a route rather than on a permutation of integers, and whatever the actual costs are, the setup is the same. Imagine a route that has just one shipment in it, the route $(1, 1)$, which is essentially an independent shipment, and a second shipment, 2, to be added: the alternatives are the places its pickup and its delivery can go, such as the pickup of 2, then the pickup of 1, then the delivery of 1, and so on, and the procedure picks the one with the minimum cost. Every time a shipment is added, the cost of the route either does not change or, more likely, increases, so all that is looked for is how to make that increase as small as possible: the cost goes up, and the procedure finds the least costly way for it to go up. If the third alternative, with cost $c_3$, is the least, and another shipment, 3, comes along, the route $(1, 2, 2, 1)$ stays in place and the procedure tries shipment 3 at each position, starting with its pickup before that of shipment 1 and its delivery right after, through all the possibilities. The number of possibilities is a formula of the route’s length before the insertion; the count can be verified on a piece of paper by listing them. In practice the procedure is of order $n^2$, about the most that can realistically be dealt with in medium to large problems, so it is at the upper limit of what is feasible. It is in some sense brute force: it uses none of the geographic information that, looking at the routes, would show that many alternatives are not worth trying. But brute force is what works for almost anything: with time windows and other constraints, it is hard to find a higher-level view of the problem that could eliminate many alternatives. The procedure leaves out the alternatives in which the truck goes empty between shipments, for example the pickup and delivery of shipment 1 followed by the pickup of shipment 2: whenever the truck becomes empty, what follows is defined as a second route, which also reduces the possibilities quite a lot. The efficiency of the procedure can be improved by techniques from computer science, the main one being memoization: when a route is expensive to evaluate, as with time windows, where the route has to be scanned, its cost can be stored in a Julia dictionary with the route as its key, as infinity if it is infeasible, so that the next time the route is seen its cost is looked up rather than computed. Improving efficiency on the programming side, rather than with domain knowledge that applies only to one type of problem, is typically much more robust.

The pickup of the new shipment goes into one of the $m + 1$ gaps of a route of $m$ stops, before its first stop, between two of its stops, or after its last, and the delivery into the same gap or a later one. Two of those positions are not routes: loading and unloading the new shipment before the first stop, or after the last, leaves the truck empty between it and the other shipments, and by constraint (c) of Model 1 that makes two routes. So the number of routes evaluated is

$$
\frac{m(m + 3)}{2} - 1
\tag{5}
$$

where

- $m$ = number of stops on the route before the insertion, two per shipment.

Minimum cost insertion does not try those two positions. Of the six positions for inserting shipment 2 into the route $(1, 1)$, four are routes, and of the 15 for inserting a third shipment into a route of two shipments, 13 are.

Given a load sequence $L$, the procedure insertimprove, formulated below, is used to construct a route $R$. Each shipment $y$ in $L$ is added to $R$ using the subprocedure mincostinsert that determines where the loading and unloading of the shipment can be added with the minimum increase in cost.

Model 1 formulation: Minimum cost insertion

```text
algorithm mincostinsert;
{ input:  shipment y; route R of m = 2n stops; cost c(R)             }
{ output: R with y loaded and unloaded at least cost, and its cost   }
begin
    TC := ∞;
    for i := 1 to m do                  { the gap y is loaded in   }
        for j := max(2, i) to m + 1 do  { the gap y is unloaded in }
        begin
            R′ := (z₁, …, zᵢ₋₁, y, zᵢ, …, zⱼ₋₁, y, zⱼ, …, zₘ);
            if c(R′) < TC then R* := R′, TC := c(R′);
        end;
    return R*, TC;
end;
```

In mincostinsert, $y$ is inserted between subsequences of $R$, where any subsequence $\left(z_i,\ldots,z_j\right)$ where $i > j$ corresponds to the empty sequence $\left(\,\right)$; thus, for example, when $i = 1$ and $j = 2$, $\left(z_1, z_0, y, z_1, z_1, y, z_2,\ldots,z_{|R|}\right)$ reduces to $\left(y, z_1, y, z_2,\ldots,z_{|R|}\right)$, a route where the loading of the new shipment occurs before any of the other shipments in the sequence.

The implementation runs the loops above as written, evaluating only the routes counted by Eq. 5, as a function named apart from Logjam’s, mincostinsert_rte: Logjam’s mincostinsert, in the release the course’s environment pins, also tries $i = j = m + 1$, loading and unloading the new shipment after the last stop, which is not a route.

Model 1 implementation: Minimum cost insertion

```julia
# Model: route sequencing, minimum cost insertion
function mincostinsert_rte(idx, rte, rteTCh)
    rteᵒ, TCᵒ = copy(rte), Inf
    for i = 1:length(rte)
        for j = max(2,i):length(rte) + 1
            rte′ = vcat(rte[1:i-1], idx, rte[i:j-1], idx, rte[j:end])
            TC = rteTCh(rte′)
            if TC < TCᵒ
                rteᵒ, TCᵒ = rte′, TC
            end
        end
    end
    return rteᵒ, TCᵒ
end
```

```text
mincostinsert_rte (generic function with 1 method)
```

Example 3: Minimum cost insertion

Determine where minimum cost insertion loads and unloads shipment 2 in the route $(1, 1)$, and then shipment 3 in the result, for the shipments of Fig. 1 and for those of Ex. 2.

Example 3(a): Three shipments on one route

Determine every route the two insertions evaluate for the shipments of Fig. 1, and the least costly of each.

Ex. 2 has reused the names D and sh, so Code block 16 finds Ex. 1’s costs again from the network g of Code block 2, which Ex. 2 left unchanged, and enters Ex. 1’s shipments again, as D1 and sh1:

```julia
# Code block 16: Ex. 1's costs and shipments, again
D1 = Int.(shortestpaths(g, weights(g), nv(g))[1])  # g of Code block 2
sh1 = DataFrame(b = [1, 3, 5], e = [2, 4, 6])
rTD1h(rte) = rteTC(rte, sh1, D1);
```

Code block 17 is minimum cost insertion written out to print every route it evaluates, as $(i, j)$, the route and its cost:

```julia
# Code block 17: insertion, printing every route it evaluates
function mincostinsert_prt(idx, rte, rteTCh)
    rteᵒ, TCᵒ = copy(rte), Inf
    for i = 1:length(rte)
        for j = max(2,i):length(rte) + 1
            rte′ = vcat(rte[1:i-1], idx, rte[i:j-1], idx, rte[j:end])
            TC = rteTCh(rte′)
            println(i,",",j,": ",rte′, " = ", TC)
            if TC < TCᵒ
                rteᵒ, TCᵒ = rte′, TC
            end
        end
    end
    return rteᵒ, TCᵒ
end

# insert shmt 2 route into shmt 1 route
rte12, TD12 = mincostinsert_prt(2, [1, 1], rTD1h)
@show rte12
@show TD12
# insert shmt 3 route into shmt 1&2 route
rte123, TD123 = mincostinsert_prt(3, rte12, rTD1h)
@show rte123
@show TD123;
```

The pseudocode is not meant to be understood in every detail; it gives the flavor of the procedures, and it is cleaner than the Julia code, which for these problems becomes messy enough to give little insight into what is happening, while mapping closely to what that code does. At the highest level, a routing procedure takes minimum cost insertion and the sequence $L$ of the shipments the route is to be created from, and the order in which the shipments are considered gives different routes. Online, there is probably no control over that order: the shipments are taken in whatever order they appear, each is inserted at minimum cost, and the resulting route is passed to 2-opt. Offline, different orderings of the shipments would be tried, to see which is best. Minimum cost insertion itself is just two nested for loops, literally trying all of the possibilities, with $c$ evaluating the cost of each route; though written as a function of $R$ alone, $c$ could be a complicated procedure, taking all kinds of capacity considerations into account.

After each shipment has been inserted into $R$, the pairwise exchange subprocedure twoopt is used to possibly improve the route by replacing nonconsecutive pairs of segments $\left(z_{i-1}, z_i\right)$ and $\left(z_j, z_{j+1}\right)$ in $R$ with segments $\left(z_{i-1}, z_j\right)$ and $\left(z_i, z_{j+1}\right)$, and reversing the subsequence $\left(z_i,\ldots,z_j\right)$ until a reduction in cost is found; if so, $R$ is replaced with the improved route and the process restarts, continuing until no improvement is found for all pairs of segments.

The 2-opt of Lecture 5.1 never moves the first or the last element of the sequence it improves, which for a tour is the depot at both ends. On a route those are its first and last stops, and moving them is part of improving it, so the 2-opt of a route reverses any stretch $(z_i, \ldots, z_j)$ of it, as described above, its first and last stops included. A reversal can also leave the truck empty between shipments, as $(1, 2, 1, 2)$ reversed in its middle gives $(1, 1, 2, 2)$, two routes, so a reversal that does is skipped; rtesegsum of Code block 4 gives the shipments on board over each segment:

Model 1 formulation: Modified two-opt

```text
algorithm twoopt;
{ input:  route R = (z₁, …, zₘ) of m = 2n stops; cost c(R)          }
{ output: route Rᵒ that no 2-opt change improves, and its cost TCᵒ  }
begin
    Rᵒ := R, TCᵒ := c(R);              { the start is the best so far  }
    done := false;
    while not done do                  { until a scan improves nothing }
    begin
        done := true, i := 1;
        while done and i ≤ m − 1 do
        begin
            j := i + 1;
            while done and j ≤ m do
            begin
                R′ := R with zᵢ, …, zⱼ reversed;    { a 2-opt change }
                if R′ carries a shipment over every segment
                   and c(R′) < TCᵒ then            { strictly better }
                    Rᵒ := R′, TCᵒ := c(R′), done := false;
                j := j + 1;
            end;
            i := i + 1;
        end;
        R := Rᵒ;                       { scan again from the new route }
    end;
    return Rᵒ, TCᵒ;
end;
```

Model 1 implementation: Modified two-opt

```julia
# Model: route sequencing, modified two-opt, the twoopt of a route
function twoopt_rte(r, rTCh)
    rᵒ, TCᵒ = copy(r), rTCh(r)
    done = false
    while !done
        done = true
        for i = 1:length(r)-1, j = i+1:length(r)
            r′ = vcat(r[1:i-1], reverse(r[i:j]), r[j+1:end])
            all(>(0), rtesegsum(r′, ones(maximum(r′)))) || continue
            TC = rTCh(r′)
            if TC < TCᵒ
                rᵒ, TCᵒ = r′, TC
                done = false
                break
            end
        end
        r = copy(rᵒ)
    end
    return rᵒ, TCᵒ
end
```

```text
twoopt_rte (generic function with 1 method)
```

Insert and improve, the online procedure, is these two in turn, shipment by shipment in the order of $L$:

Model 1 formulation: Insert and improve

```text
algorithm insertimprove;
{ input:  load sequence L of n shipments; cost c(R) }
{ output: route R and its cost                      }
begin
    R := (y, y), where y is the first shipment of L;
    for each later shipment y of L, in order, do
    begin
        R := mincostinsert(y, R);     { minimum cost insertion }
        R := twoopt(R);               { modified two-opt       }
    end;
    return R, c(R);
end;
```

Model 1 implementation: Insert and improve

```julia
# Model: route sequencing, insert and improve
function insertimprove(L, rTCh)
    r = [L[1], L[1]]
    for k in L[2:end]
        r = mincostinsert_rte(k, r, rTCh)[1]
        r = twoopt_rte(r, rTCh)[1]
    end
    return r, rTCh(r)
end
```

```text
insertimprove (generic function with 1 method)
```

Infeasibility is handled the way it was in the location problems: there are more elegant ways of accounting for it, but whenever a route is not feasible its cost is set to infinity, and the computer does the work. The difficulty, as with location, is that in some cases just getting a feasible starting point is hard: a point picked at random is likely to be infeasible, and a search started there, like the Nelder-Mead search of Lecture 2.2, just spins its wheels, still reporting infinity, and gets nowhere. That is why it is important to have a good construction procedure, one that, whatever the problem, builds a solution piece by piece and keeps it feasible, which for complicated problems is the hardest thing. A small trucking company, for example, might care nothing about the optimality of its routes, since it already has its trucks, and want only routes that are feasible, because getting one by hand that does not violate any of its many constraints is already a struggle; feasibility can be much more of a priority than any notion of optimality. As each shipment is added, different shipment orders can result in different routes, and 2-opt improves each with the first improvement procedure of Lecture 5.1: as soon as a better route is found, it becomes the new route and the improvement starts again from it. The alternative, steepest descent, tries all possibilities and takes the best of them, then tries all possibilities again; first improvement tends to work better.

The total cost of each route created by the procedure is dependent on the order of the shipment sequence $L$. For example, referring to the three shipments shown in Fig. 1, there are six different possible sequences $L$.

NoteCost allocation for routing

Cost allocation for routing arises when shipments from different firms share the same vehicle: how much should each shipment contribute to the total cost paid to the carrier? That is not the typical case in practice. Typically the carrier runs the whole show: it hires the truck, gets a variety of customers, determines how to combine and route their shipments, and determines what to charge each of them, whether a standard posted price or a price the shipper can take or leave. The scenario can be flipped, to a coalition of shippers that rents a vehicle for their transportation, and the question then is how to split its cost among them in a way that is fair. That question has applications well beyond routing, and there is no standard definition of what is fair: it depends on what is important. What makes the routing problem easier is that it has a natural reservation price, a shipment’s best alternative, which is its independent charge, TL or LTL. Since even a really small shipment can always ship LTL, no shipper would agree to be charged more than that, and the allocation is bounded by it. And unlike a manufacturer’s costs, which it seldom reveals, TL and LTL charges are largely public, at least as spot prices, which are the worst case, since a shipper with enough volume pays a negotiated discount off them. Two shipments, each a truckload over the same 300 miles at \$1 per mile, cost \$300 each shipped independently; if together they need no more than one truck’s maximum payload, they can share one truck and split its \$300, while shipments that each fill a truck gain nothing by collaborating.

A mechanism for that flipped scenario uses publicly available information about the shipments to consolidate several of them into a single load. Its routes are built online: as each new shipper joins a coalition, an online route construction procedure with 2-opt improvement reconstructs the route, and the new transport charge is reallocated to each shipper, which lets a shipper determine its own share of the charge when it wants to be part of more than one consolidated load.1

That is insert and improve, used online in earnest: each shipper’s shipment is inserted at least cost as it joins, and the route is improved by 2-opt.

Which allocation is fair turns out to depend on the horizon. Of two allocation methods, Shapley and proportional, the Shapley allocation is the most equitable in the short term, when a fixed set of shipments is to be consolidated, since it charges each shipment a cost that closely matches its impact on the overall cost of the consolidated load; proportional allocation promotes efficiency in the long term, because it gives shippers an incentive to consolidate more.2

Equity and efficiency pulling apart is the trade-off of the apartment problem of Model 4 in Lecture 2.1, where the fair location cost the couple more travel in total than the efficient one, the price of fairness.

## 3. Savings

Lecture 5.1 defined the pairwise saving of two customers served from a DC, Eq. 8 in Lecture 5.1: the cost of serving them individually, by two round trips, less the cost of serving them together on one route. The savings procedures of this section are built on it, and on its generalization to two shipments that each have their own origin and destination.

Pairwise savings are what the offline procedures are built on, and of those the savings procedure is probably the best. It calculates the pairwise savings between shipments. For the two shipments 1 and 2 of Fig. 6, the separate costs are 300 and 250, and combined the cost is 30 + 250 + 30 = 310, the green route that carries 1 and 2 together. The pairwise saving is the cost of the two as individual point-to-point shipments less their cost shipped together, here 300 + 250 − 310 = 240. Most savings procedures calculate all of the pairwise savings and then construct a route by picking the largest. What subtracts from a saving is the extra distance traveled with fewer shipments on board: here, 30 miles to pick up the second shipment and, after dropping it off, another 30 to drop off the first. So savings are largest when two shipments have the same origin and the same destination, and none can do better than that; of such pairs, the procedure would start with the pair whose origin and destination are furthest apart, the pair most worth shipping together, and work back from it.

The pairwise savings between shipments $i$ and $j$, and that of shipments 1 and 2, are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
s_{ij} &= c_i + c_j - c_{ij} \\
s_{1,2} &= 300 + 250 - 310 = 240
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
$$

where

- $s_{ij}$ = pairwise savings between shipments $i$ and $j$
- $c_i$ = cost of shipment $i$ shipped independently
- $c_{ij}$ = cost of the least costly route carrying shipments $i$ and $j$ together.

A saving is negative when the two shipments cost more together than apart, and the savings procedures list only the positive ones.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia

    # the roads among locations 1 to 4
```

Figure 6: The pairwise saving of shipments 1 and 2 of Fig. 1. Shipped independently (blue), they cost 300 and 250; on one route (green), which loads 1 and then 2 and unloads 2 and then 1, they cost 30 + 250 + 30 = 310.

The savings procedure this section ends with allows pickups and deliveries at different points, and puts a shipment anywhere in a route, because it uses minimum cost insertion, which is easy with today’s computers. In 1964, Clarke and Wright proposed a savings procedure that was computationally feasible for its time, by only adding shipments at the beginning or the end of a route: there was no way of putting a shipment in the middle of a route, since that is minimum cost insertion, which on the computers of the 1960s would not have been computationally feasible. Remarkably, it works really well, and even today it gives a pretty good solution, still computationally reasonable some 60 years later. It calculates the savings just as above, the same notion of a saving, and looks at them in decreasing order of value. The only difference is what it does with each pair $i$ and $j$ of a saving: one of three things. If neither is on a route, as with the first pair, since there are no routes at the start, the two form a new route. If $i$ is not on a route and $j$ is, $i$ is considered for adding at either the beginning or the end of that route. And if $i$ and $j$ are on two different routes, the routes can only be combined if both are endpoints, each at the beginning or the end of its route; otherwise it is not possible. That third condition is where the procedure with minimum cost insertion differs: it can merge any two routes, inserting each shipment of the smaller route into the larger one by minimum cost insertion, as long as the route stays feasible. That is more complex, but for its time, Clarke-Wright was quite effective.

Clarke-Wright is the first (1964), and still best, offline routing procedure if there are only vehicle capacity constraints. The pairs of shipments are ordered in terms of their decreasing (positive) pairwise savings. Given savings pair $i$-$j$, without exceeding the capacity constraint, either: (1) create a new route if $i$ and $j$ are not in any existing route; (2) add $i$ to a route only if $j$ is at the beginning or end of the route; or (3) combine routes only if $i$ and $j$ are endpoints of each route. Rule (2) applies either way round: either shipment of the pair can be the one added, when the other is at an end of its route.

Without capacity constraints, as in this lecture, no pair is refused for exceeding a capacity, and the three rules alone determine the routes; Lecture 5.3 adds the capacity. With a depot at node 1, the saving of customers $i$ and $j$ is the pairwise saving of Eq. 8 in Lecture 5.1, written with the costs $c_{1i}$ from the depot in place of the distances $d_i$: serving them each out and back costs $2c_{1i} + 2c_{1j}$, and serving both on one route, from the depot to $i$, then to $j$ and back, costs $c_{1i} + c_{ij} + c_{j1}$, so for symmetric costs their saving is:

$$
s_{ij} = 2c_{1i} + 2c_{1j} - \left(c_{1i} + c_{ij} + c_{j1}\right) = c_{1i} + c_{1j} - c_{ij}
\tag{8}
$$

where

- $s_{ij}$ = savings of serving customers $i$ and $j$ on one route
- $c_{ij}$ = cost between nodes $i$ and $j$, node 1 the depot.

Example 5: Clarke-Wright savings

Determine the route the Clarke-Wright savings procedure constructs, without capacity constraints, from a depot at node 1 to customers at nodes 2 to 6, by hand and in Julia.

Example 5(a): By hand

Determine the savings of every pair of customers, and the route the procedure builds from them, pair by pair.

The costs between the nodes, which are symmetric, are:

$$
C = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 40 & 48 & 38 & 33 & 48 \\
40 & 0 & 87 & 46 & 65 & 75 \\
48 & 87 & 0 & 67 & 41 & 47 \\
38 & 46 & 67 & 0 & 70 & 34 \\
33 & 65 & 41 & 70 & 0 & 69 \\
48 & 75 & 47 & 34 & 69 & 0
\end{bmatrix}

$$

Node 1 is the depot, and there are five customers, nodes 2 to 6. From the distances between them, the savings are calculated. The procedure starts with the largest, nodes 4 and 6, with a saving of 52: everything else being equal, they give the biggest bang. Since the costs here are distances, it can be seen visually that these two are the closest to each other, and that is the heuristic: customers close to each other are good candidates and probably have the largest savings. As two customers get closer together, their pairwise saving gets larger, and as they get further apart it gets smaller and smaller, until, far enough apart, it goes to zero or negative; two customers at the same point have the maximum saving. The saving takes the costs of going out to each customer and back, and subtracts from their sum the cost of serving the two on one route, out to one, on to the other and back to the depot; so as the angle of separation between two customers increases, the saving goes down and down. That is the picture to have of a savings procedure: for an array of customers, with distance to be minimized, it gives a good heuristic for which customers to cluster. Neither 4 nor 6 is on a route, so they form the first route, by condition 1, since there was no route. The next pair, 3 and 6, uses condition 2, because node 6 is on the route and node 3 is not, so 3 can be added to it.

Eq. 8 gives each pair’s saving from $C$, and the procedure then takes the pairs from the largest saving down, in Table 1:

Table 1: Clarke-Wright on the five customers of Ex. 5, without capacity, pair by pair from the largest saving; the rule is the procedure’s (1) to (3), and “none” a pair already on one route.

| Step | Pair | $\boldsymbol{s_{ij} = c_{1i} + c_{1j} - c_{ij}}$ | Rule | Route |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $(4, 6)$ | $38 + 48 - 34 = 52$ | (1) new | $(1, 4, 6, 1)$ |
| 2 | $(3, 6)$ | $48 + 48 - 47 = 49$ | (2) add 3 | $(1, 4, 6, 3, 1)$ |
| 3 | $(3, 5)$ | $48 + 33 - 41 = 40$ | (2) add 5 | $(1, 4, 6, 3, 5, 1)$ |
| 4 | $(2, 4)$ | $40 + 38 - 46 = 32$ | (2) add 2 | $(1, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 1)$ |
| 5 | $(3, 4)$ | $48 + 38 - 67 = 19$ | none | |
| 6 | $(2, 6)$ | $40 + 48 - 75 = 13$ | none | |
| 7 | $(5, 6)$ | $33 + 48 - 69 = 12$ | none | |
| 8 | $(2, 5)$ | $40 + 33 - 65 = 8$ | none | |
| 9 | $(2, 3)$ | $40 + 48 - 87 = 1$ | none | |
| 10 | $(4, 5)$ | $38 + 33 - 70 = 1$ | none | |

Fig. 7 draws the starting state and the four joins. After step 4 every customer is on the one route, so the last six pairs change nothing: 2 and 5 are its two ends, and joining them would close the route without the depot.

Figure 7: Clarke-Wright on Ex. 5, the depot the tan square: (a) the starting state, each customer served out and back (gray, dotted); (b) to (e) a frame per join of Table 1, its step numbered as the table’s row is, the route in blue and the pair it joins in red.

The route costs $40 + 46 + 34 + 47 + 41 + 33 = 241$. Serving each customer out and back would cost $2(40 + 48 + 38 + 33 + 48) = 414$, and the four joins saved $52 + 49 + 40 + 32 = 173$ of it, and $414 - 173 = 241$, a Balance check of Lecture 1.2: the savings of the pairs joined account for the whole difference.

Without capacity constraints, Clarke-Wright joins customers 4 and 6, then adds 3, 5 and 2, and constructs the one route $(1, 2, 4, 6, 3, 5, 1)$, at 241.

In Julia, as by hand, the savings run from 52 down to 1, and the Clarke-Wright route, at 241, is the optimal tour.

What is remarkable is how effective the procedure is, some 60 years after Clarke and Wright proposed it in 1964. When the term savings is used for the vehicle routing problem (VRP), by default everybody thinks of the Clarke-Wright procedure; a paper on much more complex routing, calculating total logistics costs and shipment sizes with a more complex savings procedure, might draw a reviewer’s objection that the savings procedure is 60 years old. But Clarke-Wright is really just a simple version of the more complicated savings. The key thing the pairwise savings tell any savings procedure is which two nodes to start with, here nodes 4 and 6, with the largest saving, 52; the procedure then goes down the list. Node 1 is the depot and the other nodes are the customers, which is what the truck that starts and returns to Raleigh in Ex. 6(d) gives Logjam’s procedure. Each route has an empty leg that depends on whether it is peddling, where the truck loads at the depot, travels loaded and unloads at each customer, then returns empty, or collecting, where it leaves empty, makes its first, second and third pickups, and travels loaded back to the depot. Clarke-Wright cannot handle interleaved routing: it has to be collecting or peddling, the classic VRP.

The Clarke-Wright procedure of Ex. 5 has to be expanded to apply to routes with pickups and deliveries at different places. Clarke-Wright only adds a node to the beginning or to the end of a route, never anywhere in between: once a node is in a route, the points inside the route are not candidates. If the two nodes being considered are in separate routes and combining them violates no capacity, the two routes can be merged into one larger route, but again only at their beginning or end points; and if that fails, a new route is started. Those are the options, and for a route of pickups and deliveries they would not create many routes, because most of them would not be feasible. So the savings procedure for such routes looks, instead of at just the beginning and end points, at all of the places a route could be inserted: a more brute-force approach.

Written out, the savings procedure starts every shipment on a route of its own, lists the pairs with a positive saving from the largest down, and for each pair whose shipments are still on different routes, inserts the shipments of the shorter route into the longer one by minimum cost insertion, one at a time. The minimum cost insertion of Sec. 2 is used inside savings: the savings determine which shipments to combine, and mincostinsert determines where each one goes in the route it joins. So even when every shipment is known at once and the construction is offline, minimum cost insertion is needed:

Model 1 formulation: Savings

```text
algorithm savings;
{ input:  shipments 1, …, n; cost c(R), ∞ for an infeasible route }
{ output: routes, each shipment on exactly one                    }
begin
    Rₖ := (k, k) for each shipment k;
    sᵢⱼ := c(Rᵢ) + c(Rⱼ) − c(best route of i and j), each pair i < j;
    list the pairs with sᵢⱼ > 0 in decreasing order of sᵢⱼ;
    for each pair (i, j) in the list do
        if i and j are on different routes then
        begin
            S, T := the shorter and the longer of their two routes;
            R′ := T;
            for each shipment k on S do R′ := mincostinsert(k, R′);
            if c(R′) < ∞ then T := R′, S := ∅;   { the merge kept }
        end;
    return the routes that are not empty;
end;
```

Logjam exports it, with the pairwise savings as a function of its own, pairwisesavings, which lists the pairs and their savings in the order the procedure takes them.

Model 1 implementation: Savings

```julia
# Model: Route sequencing, savings construction
# rteTCh: Function that calculates route cost: rteTCh(route) -> cost.
#    Should return Inf for infeasible routes (capacity, time windows,
#    etc.).
# sh: Shipments DataFrame where each row is a shipment requiring pickup
#    and delivery.
savings    # (rteTCh, sh)
```

Example 6: Savings construction

Determine the route the savings procedure constructs for the three shipments of Fig. 1 by hand and in Julia, for the three shipments of Ex. 2, and for a tour from Raleigh to the other five cities of Ex. 2.

Example 6(a): By hand

Determine the pairwise savings of the three shipments of Fig. 1 and the routes the savings procedure merges, step by step, with the costs between their locations.

The costs between the locations, those of Code block 16, are:

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & 300 & 30 & 280 & 60 & 335 \\
300 & 0 & 280 & 30 & 335 & 60 \\
30 & 280 & 0 & 250 & 90 & 340 \\
280 & 30 & 250 & 0 & 340 & 90 \\
60 & 335 & 90 & 340 & 0 & 275 \\
335 & 60 & 340 & 90 & 275 & 0
\end{bmatrix}

$$

Each shipment shipped independently costs its own distance, $c_1 = 300$, $c_2 = 250$ and $c_3 = 275$. The least costly route of each pair is found by inserting one shipment into the other’s route, as in Fig. 3, and Eq. 7 then gives each pair’s saving, in Table 2:

Table 2: The pairwise savings of the three shipments, largest first.

| Pair $\boldsymbol{(i, j)}$ | Least costly route of the two | $\boldsymbol{c_{ij}}$ | $\boldsymbol{s_{ij} = c_i + c_j - c_{ij}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(1, 2)$ | $(1, 2, 2, 1)$, locations $(1, 3, 4, 2)$ | $30 + 250 + 30 = 310$ | $300 + 250 - 310 = 240$ |
| $(1, 3)$ | $(1, 3, 3, 1)$, locations $(1, 5, 6, 2)$ | $60 + 275 + 60 = 395$ | $300 + 275 - 395 = 180$ |
| $(2, 3)$ | $(3, 2, 2, 3)$, locations $(5, 3, 4, 6)$ | $90 + 250 + 90 = 430$ | $250 + 275 - 430 = 95$ |

The procedure takes the pairs in that order, starting from the routes $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$ and $(3, 3)$, in Table 3:

Table 3: The savings procedure on the three shipments, merge by merge.

| Step | Pair | Routes before | Merge | Route after | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $(1, 2)$, 240 | $(1, 1)$, $(2, 2)$ | Shmt 2 inserted into $(1, 1)$ | $(1, 2, 2, 1)$ | 310 |
| 2 | $(1, 3)$, 180 | $(1, 2, 2, 1)$, $(3, 3)$ | Shmt 3 inserted into $(1, 2, 2, 1)$ | $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$ | 430 |
| 3 | $(2, 3)$, 95 | $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$ | none: 2 and 3 on one route | | |

Its two merges are the two insertions of Ex. 3(a), so the procedure ends at the same route, $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$, at 430. That is the optimum of all 60 routes found by brute force in Ex. 1(c), a Landmark check: savings constructs the optimal route here, in a single pass down its list. And the 825 of the three shipped independently less the 430 is 395, more than any one pairwise saving, since the route consolidates all three.

Savings merges shipments 1 and 2 first, at a saving of 240, then shipment 3, and constructs $(3, 1, 2, 2, 1, 3)$, at 430, the optimal route.

Computing the pairwise savings in a function of its own, outside the savings procedure, makes it possible to do things to the savings rather than rely on one way of doing them. One use is diversity. The basic savings procedure always takes the savings in strictly decreasing order, so with the standard default it always constructs exactly the same route, and that route is not necessarily the optimal one; most of the time it will not be, which is why 2-opt improvement follows it. It would be nice to have the kind of randomness that picking a random starting point gave the alternating location–allocation algorithm of Lecture 2.3. To diversify the starting points, the pairwise savings are calculated, and then, going through the list, each savings value is moved to the end of the list with a probability of perhaps 5% or 10%. That makes slight changes in exactly how the route is constructed, an easy way, given the time, of getting a diverse set of constructed solutions to improve. Most of the time, though, the unchanged order probably gives the best route, so the change improves things perhaps 20 or 25% of the time: the savings procedure by itself is so good that tweaking it usually does not help, though every once in a while it does. Where a solution is needed in seconds, the order is best left alone; where there are hours of computer time, it is an easy way to let the computer explore more possibilities.

Randomized savings is a meta-heuristic, like the multi-start of Lecture 5.1: it constructs routes by savings from a randomly reordered list, improves them by 2-opt, and repeats, keeping the best. Logjam’s savings computes its list itself, so the implementation includes a savings that is given the list, Logjam’s code with that one change.

Model 1 formulation: Randomized savings

```text
algorithm randsavings;
{ input:  shipments 1, …, n; cost c(R); probability p; N starts }
{ output: best routes found, and their total cost               }
begin
    TCᵒ := ∞;
    S := the pairs with sᵢⱼ > 0, in decreasing order of sᵢⱼ;
    for k := 1 to N do
    begin
        S′ := S with each pair moved to its end with probability p;
        routes := savings, with S′ in place of S;  { construction }
        improve each route by twoopt;              { improvement  }
        if their total cost < TCᵒ then keep them, TCᵒ := that cost;
    end;
    return the routes kept, TCᵒ;
end;
```

Model 1 implementation: Randomized savings

```julia
# Model: route sequencing, randomized savings
function randreorder(ijs, p)            # each pair moved with prob. p
    mv = rand(length(ijs[1])) .< p
    return Tuple([v[.!mv]; v[mv]] for v in ijs)
end

function savings_ijs(rteTCh, sh, ijs)   # Logjam's savings, list given
    TC = nothing
    rte = [[i, i] for i in 1:nrow(sh)]
    inr = [1:nrow(sh);]
    iˢ, jˢ = ijs
    for (i, j) in zip(iˢ, jˢ)
        if inr[i] != inr[j]
            inr_src, inr_tgt =
                length(rte[inr[i]]) < length(rte[inr[j]]) ?
                (inr[i], inr[j]) : (inr[j], inr[i])
            rte′ = copy(rte[inr_tgt])
            idx_src = unique(rte[inr_src])
            for k in idx_src
                rte′, TC = mincostinsert(k, rte′, rteTCh)
                isinf(TC) && break
            end
            if !isinf(TC)
                rte[inr_tgt] = rte′
                inr[idx_src] .= inr_tgt
                rte[inr_src] = []
            end
        end
    end
    return filter!(!isempty, rte)
end

function randsavings(rteTCh, sh; p = 0.1, nruns = 30)
    ijs = pairwisesavings(rteTCh, sh)
    rteᵒ, TCᵒ = nothing, Inf
    for k = 1:nruns
        rte = savings_ijs(rteTCh, sh, randreorder(ijs, p))
        rte = [twoopt_rte(r, rteTCh)[1] for r in rte]
        TC = sum(rteTCh.(rte))
        if TC < TCᵒ
            rteᵒ, TCᵒ = rte, TC
            println(k, ": ", TCᵒ)
        end
    end
    return rteᵒ, TCᵒ
end
```

```text
randsavings (generic function with 1 method)
```

Minimum cost insertion gives different results for different orderings of the shipments, different permutations of the sequence in which they are added to the route, so it too becomes a meta-heuristic, like randomized savings: randomized insertion runs insert and improve from random load sequences and keeps the best.

Model 1 formulation: Randomized insertion

```text
algorithm randinsert;
{ input:  shipments 1, …, n; cost c(R); N starts }
{ output: best route found, and its cost         }
begin
    TCᵒ := ∞;
    for k := 1 to N do
    begin
        L := a random permutation of 1, …, n;
        R, TC := insertimprove(L);
        if TC < TCᵒ then Rᵒ := R, TCᵒ := TC;
    end;
    return Rᵒ, TCᵒ;
end;
```

Model 1 implementation: Randomized insertion

```julia
# Model: route sequencing, randomized insertion
function randinsert(rteTCh, sh; nruns = 30)
    rteᵒ, TCᵒ = nothing, Inf
    for k = 1:nruns
        rte, TC = insertimprove(randperm(nrow(sh)), rteTCh)
        if TC < TCᵒ
            rteᵒ, TCᵒ = rte, TC
            println(k, ": ", TCᵒ)
        end
    end
    return rteᵒ, TCᵒ
end
```


In some cases, everything has to be routed: every shipment goes on one route, and the question is then just the least costly way of doing it. That is route sequencing, Model 1, for all 30 shipments at once. Whether each shipment should be on a route at all, or shipped independently, is a different problem, load formation, the subject of Sec. 4.
